notes:
I've written these notes from the pages I read, and every point has its URL. Some areas came up thin:

- **Traditions with no notes:** I found nothing on Isaiah 56 from Lutheran, Pentecostal or Orthodox sources. Bible Hub lists Wesley's Notes, but I didn't read them.
- **Other sources not found:** I found nothing from the Catholic sites you listed (newadvent.org, catholic.com), bibleodyssey.org or netbible.org. The only Catholic view is the older Haydock commentary, as quoted on StudyLight.
- **Popular modern teaching:** nothing on prosperity, word of faith or hyper-grace readings of this chapter.
- **Verse 7's sacrifices and verse 8's "others":** only a little material.

---

**Background: when and to whom (scholars disagree)**
- Ellicott places the setting under King Manasseh. He thinks the king's courtiers would taunt them as aliens, and in the second case would press the letter of Deuteronomy 23:2. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/56-3.htm
- The Pulpit Commentary places it in the Babylonian exile. It thinks converts feared they would not be looked upon as equals by the native Israelites once the return came. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/56-3.htm
- The Cambridge Bible places it after the return. It blames an exclusive and intolerant spirit amongst the leaders of the new Jerusalem. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/56-3.htm
- Utley (bible.org) sees chapters 56–66 as a new section. The message turns from the exiles coming home (chs. 40–55) to faithless, covenant people in Palestine (chapters 56-66). https://bible.org/seriespage/isaiah-56

**v. 1**
- Guzik says this is spoken to discouraged people who had grown slack. God calls them to do right *before* the promised salvation comes. His example: don't wait for God to bless your finances before you start giving. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-56/
- Utley lists two commands (preserve justice, do righteousness) and two reasons (salvation is coming, righteousness will be revealed). His application is to live every day as if the Lord were coming today. https://bible.org/seriespage/isaiah-56

**v. 2**
- Guzik sees two blessings: the blessing built into obeying, and the blessing promised to the obedient under the Old Covenant. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-56/
- Utley links the "blessed man" to Psalm 1. He notes the word "keep" comes four times in the chapter (vv. 2 twice, 4, 6). https://bible.org/seriespage/isaiah-56
- Bible Hub's article ties Sabbath-keeping to moral life on the other six days too. It says profaning the Sabbath includes treating the day as spiritually trivial, not just breaking rules. https://biblehub.com/q/Meaning_of_keep_Sabbath_not_profane.htm

**Where Protestants differ: what "keeping the Sabbath" means today (vv. 2, 4, 6)**
- **Reformed (Calvin):** "Sabbath" here stands for the whole worship of God. The people kept the outward ceremony but neglected changed lives. On v. 4 he concludes that God meant not an idle ceremony but perfect holiness. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/56-6.html ; https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/56-4.html
- **Restorationist (Coffman, Churches of Christ):** "keep the sabbath" stands for every duty of the law of Moses. So the chapter's references to the Sabbath and to sacrifices are directed to Jews alone, while the welcome to eunuchs and Gentiles predicts the Messiah's kingdom. https://studylight.org/commentaries/bcc/isaiah-56.html
- **Calvary Chapel (Chuck Smith):** the Sabbath was a covenant with Israel and a shadow of things to come. So Christ has become our sabbath. Christians rest in Christ's finished work and worship on the first day of the week. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/56-6.html
- **Lord's Day keepers (Matthew Henry; Preacher's Homiletical Commentary):** the Homiletical Commentary holds that one day in seven is rightly given to God as Creator and Redeemer. Henry recalls that early Christians, asked whether they had kept the Lord's day, replied they did not dare do otherwise. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/56-4.html ; https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/56-6.html
- **Others:** Clarke reads it as keeping the day as a type of the rest that remains for the people of God. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/rhe/isaiah/56-6.html Bible Hub's study note says that while the specific observance may vary, the principle of rest and worship remains vital. https://biblehub.com/isaiah/56-6.htm

**v. 3**
- Guzik: they shouldn't say it because it isn't true. God's word outranks how they feel. He notes that eunuchs were kept from full part in temple worship (Lev. 21:17–20). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-56/
- Barnes, Poole, Gill, JFB and Benson all read this as a promise for the gospel age. The wall between Jew and Gentile comes down, and those barred by birth or ritual impurity are let in. A "dry tree" means barren, which some saw as a curse. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/56-3.htm
- **Do the eunuchs set aside Deuteronomy 23:1?** The commentators differ:
  - The Pulpit Commentary says that law shall be abrogated under the new condition of things. https://biblehub.com/isaiah/56-4.htm
  - Guzik says the promise looks ahead to the Levitical order passing away under the New Covenant. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-56/
  - The Cambridge Bible thinks the Deuteronomy rule may have targeted religious self-castration. If so, Isaiah is not overturning it but protesting its use against victims of tyranny. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/56-3.htm
- **Who are the eunuchs?** Ellicott sees them as foreign converts serving in the king's household, like Ebed-Melech. He notes that most commentators instead think of Israelites castrated by their captors, like Daniel. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/56-3.htm
- Utley points to the Ethiopian eunuch of Acts 8 as an example of this promise. https://bible.org/seriespage/isaiah-56

**v. 4**
- Calvin: true worshippers have a place in the Church even if they are eunuchs or labor under any other obstruction. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/56-4.html
- Benson says they choose God's commands freely, out of love, not out of custom or fear. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/56-3.htm

**v. 5**
- **"Memorial":** Utley says the Hebrew word is literally "hand," used as an idiom for a monument (1 Sam. 15:12; 2 Sam. 18:18). https://bible.org/seriespage/isaiah-56
- **Guzik:** a place and name with God should be enough, even without recognition from people. He quotes Wolf, who connects the verse to Yad Vashem, the Holocaust memorial in Jerusalem. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-56/
- **What the "name" is:**
  - Coffman: The name here referred to is the name, Christian. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/56-5.html
  - Gill thinks the best reading is the name "sons of God." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/56-5.htm
  - The Geneva Bible and the Pulpit Commentary take "My house" to mean the Church. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/56-5.htm
- **Singleness (Baptist, John Piper):** God promises those who remain single in Christ blessings that are better than the blessings of marriage and children. https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/single-in-christ
- **Catholic (Haydock):** now that the Church gathers people from all nations, virginity is preferable to marriage. Those who freely choose it receive greater glory. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/56-4.html

**v. 6**
- Utley lists six marks of the faithful foreigner. He calls them signs of "lifestyle faith" (Matt. 7). https://bible.org/seriespage/isaiah-56
- Barnes says that on these conditions foreigners got all the privileges of God's children. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/56-6.htm

**v. 7**
- Guzik: Israel assumed it was accepted no matter what and others were rejected no matter what. God corrects both. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-56/
- Jesus quotes this verse when he clears out the money-changers. Guzik notes they were in the outer court, the only place Gentiles could pray. Utley adds that this was the stated purpose of Solomon's temple (1 Kings 8:41–43). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-56/ ; https://bible.org/seriespage/isaiah-56
- **Sacrifices:** one older commentator on Bible Hub's 6th-verse page says the prophet had to describe the Christian era in terms of familiar temple rites. Coffman says the sacrifice language applies to Jews alone (see above). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/56-6.htm ; https://studylight.org/commentaries/bcc/isaiah-56.html
- Matthew Henry's concise commentary: people who came mourning to the house of prayer leave rejoicing. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/56-3.htm

**v. 8**
- Utley gives two readings of "others": more exiled Israelites (the Jewish JPS translation) or more outcasts such as foreigners and eunuchs. He says Jesus' use of the passage shows its wider scope. https://bible.org/seriespage/isaiah-56
- Guzik: Israel had become wrapped up in itself after the exile, and God widens its vision to a perishing world. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-56/
- Matthew Henry connects it to John 10:16, "one fold and one Shepherd." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/56-3.htm

**v. 9 (two different readings)**
- Guzik: God invites the beasts to eat the corpses of His enemies, as in Revelation 19:17. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-56/
- Utley: a parody of the feast offered in 55:1–2. Here the beasts are invited to devour God's own covenant people. https://bible.org/seriespage/isaiah-56

**v. 10**
- The Pulpit Commentary and Keil & Delitzsch say the "watchmen" are the prophets. Ellicott thinks especially of self-styled prophets. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/56-10.htm ; https://biblehub.com/isaiah/56-10.htm
- **Dogs:** Barnes says a watchdog stands for a prophet whose job is to announce danger. Keil & Delitzsch see a wordplay: instead of seers (*chozim*) they are ravers (*hozim*). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/56-10.htm
- **Applied to ministers today:**
  - Barnes thinks there was perhaps never a more vivid description of a lazy, unfaithful ministry. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/56-10.htm
  - Calvin says pastors ought to be ashamed to be outdone by a dog. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/56-10.html
  - Constable quotes E. J. Young: a minister who doesn't warn against false doctrine becomes a dog that cannot bark. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/56-10.html
- **Older Protestant polemic:** Gill applies "dreaming" to the teachings of Roman Catholic clergy. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/56-10.html

**v. 11**
- Guzik contrasts these shepherds with the godly David-like leader of 55:3–5. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-56/
- Bridgeway thinks the shepherds are the civil leaders, just as greedy as the prophets. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/56-10.html
- Pulpit Homiletics (R. Tuck) cites Philippians 2:21, "all seek their own." https://biblehub.com/sermons/isaiah/56-10.htm

**v. 12**
- Guzik: they are not just blind but wicked, getting drunk as judgment approaches. Their blind faith in progress has replaced a reasoned faith in God. He suggests it may picture an unprepared world, or even an unprepared church, at Christ's return. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-56/
- Utley: their "Come" matches the "come" of verse 9. The leaders gather to drink, and God gathers the beasts to devour. https://bible.org/seriespage/isaiah-56
